questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with 4 months of fatigue, 6kg weight loss and postural dizziness. BP 96/58 lying, 78/50 standing. You note hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and buccal mucosa. Na 128, K 5.8, glucose 3.1.
questions.lead: Which biochemical pattern do you expect on further testing?
options: ACTH high, renin high, aldosterone low
ACTH low, renin normal, aldosterone normal
ACTH high, renin low, aldosterone high
ACTH low, renin low, aldosterone high
questions.explanation: Primary adrenal insufficiency destroys the whole cortex, so both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid output fail. Loss of negative feedback drives ACTH up (hence the pigmentation — ACTH shares a precursor with MSH), and the failing zona glomerulosa means aldosterone is low with renin high as the kidney tries to compensate. That aldosterone deficit is what gives you the hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia. Option 2 is the secondary picture.
questions.point: Primary adrenal insufficiency: whole cortex fails, so ACTH is high (pigmentation) with aldosterone low and renin high — hyperkalaemia comes from the aldosterone deficit.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man on prednisolone 10mg daily for 14 months for polymyalgia rheumatica stops it abruptly. Ten days later he presents with fatigue, nausea and BP 94/60. Na 130, K 4.1, glucose 4.0. There is no hyperpigmentation.
questions.lead: Why is his potassium normal, unlike in Addison's disease?
options: Exogenous steroids suppress renal potassium excretion independently of aldosterone
Aldosterone release is driven by the renin-angiotensin system, not ACTH, so the mineralocorticoid axis is preserved
Hyperkalaemia only appears once cortisol falls below 50 nmol/L
The adrenal medulla compensates by increasing catecholamine output
questions.explanation: This is the single most examinable difference between the two. Secondary adrenal insufficiency is an ACTH problem, and ACTH only meaningfully drives the zona fasciculata. The zona glomerulosa answers to renin-angiotensin and potassium, so aldosterone keeps working — no hyperkalaemia, no hyperpigmentation. Hyponatraemia can still occur, via cortisol-deficient ADH excess rather than salt wasting.
questions.point: Secondary adrenal insufficiency spares potassium and skin colour: aldosterone runs on renin–angiotensin, not ACTH, so only the cortisol axis fails.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with known Addison's disease has had 2 days of vomiting and diarrhoea and has not kept her medications down. She is drowsy, BP 80/50 after 1L of saline, HR 122. A random cortisol has been sent and is pending.
questions.lead: What is the immediate next step?
options: Await the cortisol result before giving steroid, to avoid confounding the diagnosis
Give IV hydrocortisone 100mg now, alongside continued fluid resuscitation
Give oral hydrocortisone at double her usual dose
Start fludrocortisone and increase the dose until BP responds
questions.explanation: Adrenal crisis is treated on suspicion — never wait for the cortisol, which is drawn but not acted on. IV hydrocortisone 100mg plus aggressive fluids, and the vomiting alone rules out the oral route. Fludrocortisone is irrelevant acutely: 100mg of hydrocortisone supplies more than enough mineralocorticoid activity on its own.
questions.point: Adrenal crisis is treated on suspicion — IV hydrocortisone 100mg immediately, never waiting for the cortisol result; 100mg covers mineralocorticoid needs by itself.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with small cell lung cancer develops proximal weakness, oedema and new hypertension over 6 weeks. He is not cushingoid in appearance.
questions.lead: Which set of results fits ectopic ACTH secretion?
options: K 2.9, bicarbonate 34, glucose 12.1
K 5.9, bicarbonate 18, glucose 3.2
K 4.0, bicarbonate 24, glucose 11.8
K 2.8, bicarbonate 16, glucose 3.4
questions.explanation: Cortisol excess is the mirror image of Addison's. Massive cortisol spills over onto the mineralocorticoid receptor, giving a hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, and its counter-regulatory action gives hyperglycaemia. Option 2 is the Addisonian pattern — high K, acidosis, low glucose. Ectopic ACTH is the form most likely to present with florid biochemistry and little classic body habitus, because it moves too fast.
questions.point: Cortisol excess (e.g. ectopic ACTH) gives hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with hyperglycaemia — the exact mirror of the Addisonian high-K, acidotic, hypoglycaemic pattern.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presents with visible haematuria. He had a sore throat that started 2 days ago and is still present. BP 128/78, creatinine 88. C3 and C4 are both normal.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
IgA nephropathy
Anti-GBM disease
Thin basement membrane disease
questions.explanation: Two discriminators, both in the stem. Timing: IgA is synpharyngitic — haematuria within 1–2 days, while the throat is still sore — whereas PSGN lags the infection by 1–3 weeks. Complement: IgA runs a normal C3; PSGN runs a low C3. Thin basement membrane disease gives persistent microscopic haematuria, not visible haematuria timed to an infection.
questions.point: IgA nephropathy is synpharyngitic (haematuria within 1–2 days, sore throat still present) with normal C3; post-strep GN lags the infection by 1–3 weeks with low C3.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old presents with periorbital oedema, cola-coloured urine and BP 132/85. A sore throat resolved 2 weeks ago. C3 is low, C4 normal.
questions.lead: Which statement about the expected course is correct?
options: C3 should normalise within 8 weeks; persistent hypocomplementaemia suggests another diagnosis
C3 remains low for at least 12 months in typical disease
Steroids should be started to shorten the illness
Persistent microscopic haematuria at 6 months indicates treatment failure
questions.explanation: PSGN is managed supportively, and the complement trajectory is the follow-up test that matters: C3 normalises by 8 weeks. If it stays low, you are looking at membranoproliferative GN or lupus nephritis instead. Microscopic haematuria persisting for up to 1–2 years is normal and not failure. Steroids have no role in typical PSGN.
questions.point: Post-strep GN: C3 normalises by 8 weeks — persistent hypocomplementaemia points to MPGN or lupus nephritis instead; management is supportive, no steroids.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has an inferior STEMI. He is alert, BP 88/54, HR 52, chest clear on auscultation, JVP elevated. Right-sided leads show ST elevation in V4R. He received a GTN spray in the ambulance and his systolic fell to 70.
questions.lead: What is the appropriate immediate management?
options: Further GTN to reduce afterload, plus IV furosemide for the raised JVP
IV fluid bolus and avoidance of nitrates, with urgent reperfusion
IV metoprolol to control ischaemia
Sit him upright and start CPAP
questions.explanation: ST elevation in V4R means right ventricular infarction, and the infarcted RV is preload dependent — it cannot generate output without a high filling pressure. Nitrates, diuretics and anything else that drops preload will collapse the BP, exactly as the GTN did. Treatment is fluid loading plus reperfusion. The raised JVP here is RV failure, not volume overload — note the clear chest.
questions.point: RV infarction (inferior STEMI + ST elevation in V4R) is preload dependent: fluid load and reperfuse, never nitrates or diuretics.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman has chest pain. ECG shows ST depression of 2mm in V1–V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves. BP 138/82, chest clear. Troponin is rising.
questions.lead: What does this ECG most likely represent?
options: Anterior subendocardial ischaemia — manage as NSTEMI
Posterior STEMI — a STEMI equivalent requiring urgent reperfusion
Right ventricular infarction — withhold nitrates and load with fluid
Benign early repolarisation
questions.explanation: Anterior ST depression with tall R waves and upright T waves in V1–V3 is the mirror image of posterior ST elevation. Confirm with posterior leads V7–V9, where ≥0.5mm of elevation is diagnostic. It is a STEMI equivalent and gets the STEMI pathway, not NSTEMI timing — this is the trap. Note the discriminator from the previous question: the nitrate caution belongs to RV infarction, not posterior infarction.
questions.point: Anterior ST depression with tall R waves and upright T in V1–V3 is a posterior STEMI — confirm with V7–V9 (≥0.5mm) and treat on the STEMI pathway.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man on apixaban for non-valvular AF is scheduled for an elective right hemicolectomy. CrCl is 60 mL/min. He has no prior thromboembolic events.
questions.lead: What is the correct periprocedural anticoagulation plan?
options: Stop apixaban 48 hours pre-op; no bridging
Stop apixaban 48 hours pre-op and bridge with therapeutic LMWH
Continue apixaban throughout
Stop apixaban 5 days pre-op and bridge with LMWH
questions.explanation: Bridging is a warfarin concept — it exists because warfarin takes days to wear off and days to come back. DOACs have a short half-life and predictable offset, so stopping them at the right interval is the bridge. For high bleeding-risk surgery with CrCl ≥30, that interval is 48 hours (24 hours if low bleeding risk). Bridging a DOAC adds bleeding risk with no thrombotic benefit. The 5-day option is the warfarin answer.
questions.point: DOACs are never bridged: stop apixaban 48h before high-bleeding-risk surgery (24h if low risk, CrCl ≥30) — bridging is a warfarin concept.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is day 7 post hip replacement, on prophylactic enoxaparin. Platelets have fallen from 250 to 88. She has a new swollen right calf and ultrasound confirms DVT.
options: Cease enoxaparin and transfuse platelets given the thrombocytopenia
Cease enoxaparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as danaparoid or argatroban
Continue enoxaparin and add aspirin
Cease enoxaparin and observe; anticoagulation is unsafe below 100
questions.explanation: HIT is the counterintuitive one: despite the low platelets it is a prothrombotic state, driven by PF4-heparin antibodies that activate platelets. The timing (day 5–10), the >50% fall and new thrombosis are the 4Ts. Stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant. Never transfuse platelets — you are feeding the thrombosis. Doing nothing is equally wrong; the risk here is clot, not bleeding.
questions.point: HIT (platelet fall >50% at day 5–10 of heparin) is prothrombotic: stop all heparin, start a non-heparin anticoagulant, and never transfuse platelets.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man arrests on the ward. The monitor shows pulseless electrical activity. CPR is in progress and IV access has just been obtained.
questions.lead: Per ANZCOR guidelines, when should 1mg adrenaline be given?
options: Immediately, then every second loop
After the 2nd shock, then every second loop
After the 3rd shock, then every second loop
Only if the rhythm converts to a shockable one
questions.explanation: The adrenaline timing forks on the rhythm, which is why this keeps catching you. Non-shockable (PEA/asystole): adrenaline immediately once access is available, then every second loop. Shockable (VF/pVT): adrenaline after the 2nd shock, then every second loop. The 3rd-shock answer is amiodarone 300mg, not adrenaline — and note ANZCOR differs from UK/ERC here, which gives adrenaline after the third.
questions.point: ANZCOR non-shockable arrest (PEA/asystole): adrenaline 1mg immediately once access is in, then every second loop; in shockable rhythms it waits until after the 2nd shock.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman is in VF. She has received three shocks, adrenaline after the second, and CPR is ongoing. She remains in VF.
questions.lead: Which drug and dose is now indicated?
options: A second dose of adrenaline 1mg
Amiodarone 300mg IV
Lignocaine 100mg IV as first-line
Magnesium sulfate 10 mmol IV
questions.explanation: Amiodarone 300mg after the 3rd shock for refractory VF/pVT, with a further 150mg considered if VF persists. Adrenaline continues on its own clock — every second loop — so it is not "due" simply because a shock was delivered. Lignocaine is the alternative only if amiodarone is unavailable. Magnesium is reserved for torsades or documented hypomagnesaemia.
questions.point: Refractory VF/pVT after the 3rd shock gets amiodarone 300mg (further 150mg if persisting); adrenaline stays on its own every-second-loop cycle.

questions.stem: A 70kg man sustains burns to 25% total body surface area. He arrives in ED 2 hours after the injury. Weight-based fluid resuscitation is commenced using the Parkland formula.
questions.lead: What volume is required, and over what period?
options: 7000mL in 24 hours, with 3500mL in the first 8 hours measured from the time of injury
7000mL in 24 hours, with 3500mL in the first 8 hours measured from arrival in ED
3500mL in 24 hours, with 1750mL in the first 8 hours from arrival
7000mL in the first 8 hours, then 7000mL over the next 16 hours
questions.explanation: Parkland is 4 mL × kg × %TBSA = 4 × 70 × 25 = 7000mL of Hartmann's over 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours. The examinable subtlety is that the clock runs from the time of the burn, not from arrival — with 2 hours already elapsed, that 3500mL must go in over the remaining 6 hours, roughly 583 mL/hr. Titrate to a urine output of 0.5–1 mL/kg/hr rather than following the formula blindly.
questions.point: Parkland (4mL × kg × %TBSA, half in the first 8h) runs from the time of the burn, not arrival — titrate to urine output 0.5–1 mL/kg/hr.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is found to have a 5.8cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm on surveillance ultrasound. He is asymptomatic. He has well-controlled hypertension and is otherwise fit for surgery.
options: Continue 6-monthly ultrasound surveillance
Refer for elective repair
Repeat the scan in 12 months
Repair only if he develops back or abdominal pain
questions.explanation: The threshold for elective repair is ≥5.5cm in men (>5.0cm in women), expansion ≥1cm/year, or symptoms. At 5.8cm he is over it, and annual rupture risk now exceeds operative risk — which is the whole logic of the cut-off. Waiting for pain is waiting for the aneurysm to declare itself, by which point you are operating on a symptomatic or ruptured AAA at far higher mortality.
questions.point: AAA repair is elective at ≥5.5cm in men (>5.0cm women), expansion ≥1cm/year, or symptoms; below that, surveillance — operative risk exceeds rupture risk.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is brought in after a high-speed motorcycle crash. He is making gurgling sounds, GCS is 7 (E1 V2 M4), SpO2 88% on 15L non-rebreather. BP 110/70, HR 96. The trauma CT scanner is available and free.
questions.lead: Following ATLS principles, what happens next?
options: Transfer immediately to CT to identify the head injury
Suction and definitive airway management with rapid sequence intubation
Insert an oropharyngeal airway and proceed to the secondary survey
Obtain a chest X-ray and pelvic X-ray first
questions.explanation: ABCDE is a priority order, not a checklist to complete before acting — you fix each problem as you find it. Gurgling plus GCS 7 is a failure to protect the airway, and that is an A problem, so it is addressed before anything in B, C or D. A definitive airway means a cuffed tube below the cords; an OPA does not protect against aspiration. CT is the classic distractor — never take an unstable or unprotected airway to the scanner.
questions.point: ATLS fixes each problem as it is found: an unprotected airway (GCS ≤8, gurgling) means RSI and a cuffed tube before anything else — never straight to CT.
